rv.q: Noises Off remains as reliable an engine of joy as there is on the British stage, rendered with the precision wallop that the director Lindsay Posner offers in what is as good a revival as I've seen of one of the funniest, most cannily structured plays in the canon.
It's the pain behind the slapstick that strikes you in Lindsay Posner's beautifully observed production.
But mostly Noises Off is just blissfully, brilliantly funny.
This is a superior revival to the one seen in 2019, with a sense – spurred by the pandemic? – of top-rank stage-actors relishing the deranging peculiarity of their profession.
If Lindsay Posner's current production isn't quite as sharp as his delectable 2011 version, which premiered at the Old Vic before a West End transfer, then no matter.
Acts I and III, featuring events front of stage, are mildly amusing. Act II, when we see the panic and calamities backstage, can be the stuff of genius.
Solidly entertaining, then; it just doesn't take your breath away.
Basically, 'Noises Off' is both timeless and dated and I honestly think that it's a rare play that would probably benefit from a straight-up modern remake.
The entire thing breezes away the January blues with glorious brilliance. It is an utter treasure.
Not one cast member can be faulted for their performances as they were all impeccable.
Tracy-Ann Oberman, on utterly majestic form as know-it-all pro Belinda... Just fabulous.
It is in this third aspect that the production scores in a way that gives it its contemporary relevance.
